claims.text: The initial NbZrTiHfMo alloy is equiatomic.
The initial equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy has a single-phase disordered BCC structure.
The initial alloy has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
The initial alloy has limited room-temperature compressive plasticity.
Approximately 20% of the Mo content can be replaced by V while preserving the overall alloy balance.
A 20% replacement of Mo by V can preserve a single-phase disordered BCC structure and compositional homogeneity under suitable processing conditions.
Partial substitution of Mo with V reduces the overall electronegativity differences among the constituent elements.
The reduced electronegativity difference moderates lattice distortion.
The reduced electronegativity difference enhances dislocation mobility.
Replacing Mo with V reduces overly strong solute-dislocation interactions or local bonding inhomogeneities.
Strong solute-dislocation interactions or local bonding inhomogeneities limit the alloy's ductility.
Residual lattice distortion after V substitution will continue to provide high yield strength.
Approximately 20% replacement of Mo by V will improve plastic strain to failure by about 10–30% relative to the equiatomic alloy.
Approximately 20% replacement of Mo by V will retain compressive yield strength within about 10% of 1719 MPa.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect is limited to modest V substitution near 20% of the original Mo content and to processing that preserves a single-phase disordered BCC structure.
Excessive V substitution or processing deviations may cause phase instability or a notable loss of strength.

contradictions.description: The predicted plasticity improvement is 10–30%, whereas the falsification rule gives an ambiguous 10–20% minimum-improvement range rather than one fixed cutoff, so outcomes between 10% and 20% cannot be classified decisively.
